newsitem.title: USA: Gore said nothing illegal in his fund-raising.
newsitem.headline: Gore said nothing illegal in his fund-raising.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore on Monday said he was proud of his role in raising funds for U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election and insisted he broke no laws in pressing for political contributions.

In a hastily called news conference at the White House that was designed to quell a growing uproar over his fund-raising activities, Gore calmly told reporters that he had closely adhered to all legal requirements.

"I'm proud of what I did," Gore said. "I do not feel like I did anything wrong, much less illegal. I am proud to have done everything I possibly could to help support the re-election of this president."

Gore acknowledged that he made "a few" telephone calls from his White House office to potential contributors asking for donations to the Democratic National Committee (DNC). He said the calls were charged to a DNC credit card so that the expense was not paid by the federal government.
Under the Hatch Act, enacted to prevent federal officials from using government facilities and employees for re-election purposes, fund-raising activity may not be conducted on federal property.

Gore, noting that he and the president are exempt from the provisions of the act, said that his legal counsel -- Charles Burson -- "advises me that there is no controlling, legal authority or case that says that there was any violation of law whatsoever."
Acknowledging a problem with the public's perception of his telephone calls, Gore said he "decided to adopt a policy of not making any such calls ever again."

"If there had been a shred of doubt in my mind that anything I did was a violation of law, I assure you, I would not have done that," said Gore, who has enjoyed a reputation of integrity throughout his political career.

The Washington Post generated questions on Sunday about Gore's fund-raising activities during the past presidential campaign and said the vice president became known among Democratic Party officials as the administration's "soliciter-in-chief."
Gore insisted he had never heard the description and brushed aside the newspaper's account that some Democratic Party donors were offended that he was twisting their arms for donations.

"I cannot explain to you what some anonymous source wants to say," Gore said. "I can tell you this, that I never, ever said or did anything that would have given rise to a feeling like ... I never did that, and I never would do that."

He renewed the administration's call for campaign finance reform to end many of the practices followed by the Clinton campaign -- particularly so-called "soft money" donations to political parties that now are exempt from spending limits.

Both Democrats and Republicans raised record amounts of money for the 1996 presidential election and congressional campaigns, where nearly $2.7 billion was spent in the most expensive campaigning in the nation's history.
A Senate committee and a House panel are preparing to investigate campaign abuses, centering for the most part on Democratic fund raising.
Attorney General Janet Reno has rejected requests for a special independent counsel to investigate fund raising, saying it was not warranted at this point.

Appearing on CNN's "Crossfire" on Monday, former Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour said the vice president's actions were clearly in violation of a federal law banning use of federal offices for fund raising, and he urged Gore to give more details on his activities.
On the same programme, former Clinton adviser Dick Morris said Gore's efforts helped win the election and prevent passage of key Republican legislation.
He also said six current Republican senators whom he previously advised had solicited funds from their Senate offices -- in his presence. He did not reveal their names.
